## Introduction

This course is about behavioural interventions. It draws on research from behaviour analysis, education, psychology, rehabilitation, and public health, to explore evidence-informed tactics for helping people change their behaviour.

Primarily, the book has been designed as a resource for my students as a companion to the taught sessions. The sequence of chapters mirrors the structure of the lectures. While I developed the book with my students in mind, you are very welcome to use it if you find it to be helpful.

## The Circumstances View of Behaviour

A defining feature of the behaviour analytic approach to understanding behaviour is its emphasis on environmental contingencies. Behaviour analysts attend to the context in which behaviour occurs and its function, rather than explaning it in terms of traits, dispositions or hypothetical mental states. This approach represents a methodological commitment to seeking explanations at the level of behaviour-environment relations. A practical advantage of this approach is that enironmental variables are often observable and manipulable, making functional analysis and experimental control more tractable [see @friman2021].

Explanations that attribute behaviour to internal factors are typically descriptive rather than functional. They often lead to restating observations in dispositional terms (e.g., This student does not attend because they are unmotivated), which offer little guidance in what might be changed to influence behaviour. A circumstances view of behaviour, by contrast, asks, Which environmental events are evoking and maintaining this pattern of behaviour?", and "what adaptations might be needed for behaviour to change?". This reframing can be practically helpful. For the student who is unmotivated, we might find that instructional tasks are too difficult or that competing activities are preferred.   

## Principles as Tools

The core toolkit of a behaviour analyst consists of predictable relationships between behaviour and the environment, established through decades of research in operant conditioning. These relationships tell us how behaviour is likely to change when environmental conditions change. Using them to predict and influence behaviour is what puts the analysis in applied behaviour analysis 

Understanding that a behaviour is maintained by intermittent positive reinforcement, for instance, enables a practitioner to predict how someone will respond to changes in the reinforcement schedule, what removal or witholding of reinforcement will look like, and what stimuli might come to acquire control over the behaviour. The practitioner who understands how to use these principles as tools is better positioned to design effective interventions but also to anticipate difficulties and revise strategies wheere neccessary.

The tactics presented in the chapters that follow are drawn from the evidence base on behaviour analytic interventions and applications. The empirical literature on behavioural intervention is both rich and exapnding, but it is not uniform; the quality and quantity of studies is often variable. This is a topic that I have explored at length in some of my own research work here: @may2022; and here: @may2026. Accordingly, a recurring concern throughout the book is the quality and status of the evidence underpinning the various approaches covered. The reader will therefore find, alongside practical guidance, an introduction to some of the tools needed to evaluate evidence and claims critically. It is also worth saying that this course isn't a comprehensive theoretical or philosophical treatment of behaviour analysis. There are plenty of resources exploring those domains elsewhere [@catania2013; @skinner1953]. 


## Why Programmed Instruction?

Programmed Instruction is built on the idea that learning is maximised when it is arranged deliberately, systematically, and in close contact with reinforcement. Fundamentally, Programmed Instruction arranges learning material as a sequence of small and carefully designed steps where learners respond actively throughout.

Programmed Instruction emerged from efforts to apply behavioural principles to education. The idea being that, if behaviour is shaped by its consequences, then effective instruction should ensure that responding and feedback are both maximised. Programmed instruction does exactly this. The content in this book is broken into manageable units called *frames*, each requiring a response, and followed immediately by feedback. 

## Active Responding

A hallmark of Programmed Instruction is its shift from passive consumption to active responding. Here, knowledge aquisiton is of a repertoire of behavior which is built and reinforced. This reconceptualises the learner as an active participant not a passive bystander. Instant confirmation of a correct response functions as reinforcement, while contingent correction prevents the rehearsal of errors. The loop of action and feedback builds the  foundation necessary for the development of fluency.

## Sequencing and Discrimination

I have tried to organise the material in a way so that concepts are introduced and develop in a logical way. Earlier frames establish the prerequisites for later ones. Critical distinctions are revisited multiple times across different contexts in an attempt to promote discrimination between, and generalisation within, concepts. 
For learners preparing for certification in behaviour analysis, these features are especially valuable. Passing the professional certification examinations requires that you have a fluent repertoire of a vast array of terms and definitions. 

## Self-Paced and Learner-Controlled

Programmed Instruction is also designed to be self-paced and learner-controlled. You can progress through the course material at a rate determined by your own performance. This might involve spending more time where needed (e.g., reviewing previous frames or course readings) and gliding through material they you find easier. This means that the approach respects the real differences between learners while maintaining consistent instructional quality.

## The Evidence Base

The design principles underlying this book are supported by converging evidence from three bodies of research.

The first is behaviour analysis itself. Programmed Instruction emerged directly from Skinner's experimental analysis of behaviour and develoiped out of a program of applied research across educational and clinical environments [@skinner1958; @kulik1979]. It is a well established that active responding, immediate feedback, and carefully arranged contingencies produce more durable learning than passive exposure.

The second is the literature on retrieval practice. Retrieval refers to the behaviour of recalling information, as opposed to re-reading or reviewing it passively. A substantial body of research demonstrates that retrieval practice produces significantly better long-term retention than passive study, an effect which has replicated across age groups, subject matter, and educational contexts. The active responding elements of this book are retrieval practice by another name. [@rowland2014; @adesope2017; @agarwal2021].

The third design principle is spaced-practice and interleaving. Distributing (or spacing) practice across time improves retention when compared to massed practice [@cepeda2006]. Similarly, interspersing related but distinct concepts during practice (i.e., interleaving) improves discrimination between, and generalisation within, concepts [@brunmair2019; @firth2021]. The sequencing of frames in this book, in which concepts are revisited across sections in varied contexts, reflects the incorporation of both of these principles.

## When a "Mistake" is Actually Helpful

Occasionally, you might enter an answer that is technically correct, but the feedback will ask you to try again. This is because the program doesn't recognise the specific term that you entered. While this can feel frustrating, this is a feature of the system that can actually be beneficial for learning. The moment of surprise this creates is known as a prediction error: a mismatch between what you expected (that your answer would be accepted) and what actually happened. It is a consistent finding that prediction errors are a powerful driver of learning[@Schultz2016; @RescorlaWagner1972;  @Kornell2009; @Reuter2019].

Paradoxically, when an outcome is unexpected, it captures attention and strengthens memory for the correct response. So, if you are asked to retype an answer, think of it this way: What might feel like a small obstacle is actually doing useful work behind the scenes. Thus, you can think of it as feature of the system, rather than a bug!

If you get an incorrect response, first review the feedback and check that you entered your answer correctly. Then review the previous frames that you have completed. If you are confident your entry is correct, try to think of an alternative word that conveys the same meaning within the context of the sentence. If you are still unsure, please don’t hesitate to reach out for support. 

## How to Use This Book

To summarise, you will be asked to respond frequently thorughout the book. If you find the format a little demanding, that is by design. My aim is to prompt responding that will help the targeted repertoires to be understood and retained.

Each time you correctly complete a chapter, you will unlock access to a section of the site called The Token Exchange. On this page, you will be invited to complete five multiple-choice questions based on the chapter content, with opportunities to potentially win prizes. You can read more about (and access) the Token Exchange here:[Token Exchange](slot-machine.qmd)

Lastly, this site is very much a work in progress, so if you happen to notice any mistakes then you can help by emailing me at richard.may@southwales.ac.uk.


::: callout-important
## Before you begin

Approach each frame actively. Attempt a response before checking the answer. Treat errors as opportunities to refine your understanding by reviewing the material - not as failures. Over time, the repeated contact with these contingencies will produce a repertoire of behaviour that passive study methods rarely achieve.

:::
